item.title: 5 Books you must read to learn how to say no confidently
item.description: Discover five books that teach you to say no confidently, set healthy boundaries, overcome people-pleasing and protect your peace of mind.
item.content:encoded:
Saying no can be surprisingly difficult, especially when you worry about disappointing others, damaging relationships or being perceived as selfish.

Whether it is agreeing to extra work, accepting social invitations you would rather decline or constantly putting other people's needs before your own, the habit of saying yes can leave you feeling overwhelmed and emotionally exhausted.

Learning to set boundaries does not mean becoming rude or uncaring. It means recognising your limits, respecting your time and understanding that you cannot meet everyone's expectations.

The right books can help you understand people-pleasing, communicate your needs more clearly and become comfortable with the possibility that not everyone will agree with your decisions.

If you find yourself struggling to say no without feeling guilty, these five books offer practical insights into building boundaries, protecting your energy and developing healthier relationships.

5 Books you must read to learn how to say no confidently

1. The Joy of Saying No by Natalie Lue

If guilt often prevents you from saying no, Natalie Lue's The Joy of Saying No is a useful place to begin. The book explores people-pleasing, emotional obligations and the fear of disappointing others. It encourages readers to recognise when they agree to things out of guilt rather than genuine willingness.

Lue also highlights the importance of understanding your limits and communicating them without overexplaining every decision. Learning to say no becomes easier when you stop treating everyone else's approval as a responsibility.

The book reminds readers that protecting their time and emotional well-being is not an act of selfishness.

2. Set Boundaries, Find Peace by Nedra Glover Tawwab

In Set Boundaries, Find Peace, therapist Nedra Glover Tawwab explains why healthy boundaries are essential for maintaining balanced relationships. The book explores how unclear expectations can contribute to resentment, frustration and emotional exhaustion.

Through practical guidance, Tawwab helps readers identify their needs, communicate limits and respond when others struggle to respect them. It covers boundaries in family relationships, friendships, romantic partnerships and professional settings.

For anyone who finds it difficult to refuse requests from loved ones, this book offers a helpful reminder that caring about someone does not require agreeing with everything they ask.

3. When I Say No, I Feel Guilty by Manuel J. Smith

Manuel J. Smith's When I Say No, I Feel Guilty focuses on assertiveness and the ability to communicate your thoughts without becoming aggressive or unnecessarily apologetic. It helps readers understand how fear, social pressure and the desire for approval can make ordinary conversations difficult.

The book introduces practical communication techniques for handling criticism, unreasonable requests and attempts to pressure you into changing your decision. Its central approach is to help readers express themselves calmly while respecting both their own rights and those of others.

It is particularly useful for people who struggle to stand their ground during uncomfortable conversations.

4. Essentialism: The Disciplined Pursuit of Less by Greg McKeown

Greg McKeown's Essentialism explores how to focus on what genuinely matters instead of spreading your time and energy across too many commitments. The book challenges the assumption that being productive means doing more and accepting every opportunity.

Also Read
5 Teachings from Essentialism about doing less but better

McKeown encourages readers to distinguish between essential priorities and activities that contribute little to their goals. This approach makes saying no easier because decisions become guided by what matters most rather than by pressure to please everyone.

For professionals, students and anyone managing competing responsibilities, the book offers a practical way to protect time and make more intentional choices.

5. The Book of Boundaries by Melissa Urban

Melissa Urban's The Book of Boundaries provides practical guidance for communicating personal limits in everyday situations. It addresses challenges involving family members, friends, colleagues and other people who may have expectations that conflict with your needs.

One of the book's most useful aspects is its focus on what to say when setting a boundary. Having clear language can make difficult conversations less intimidating, particularly when you are accustomed to agreeing automatically.

Urban encourages readers to communicate their limits clearly and follow through consistently, rather than relying on others to guess what makes them uncomfortable.

Final thoughts

Learning to say no is not about shutting people out or refusing every request. It is about understanding your priorities, recognising your limits and making decisions without constantly seeking approval.

These five books approach the subject from different perspectives, including people-pleasing, assertive communication, healthy relationships and time management. Together, they offer practical ways to establish boundaries and become more confident about expressing your needs.

item.title: Can AI make debt collections less about chasing and more about predicting?
item.description: The future lies in using data to understand portfolios, AI to prioritise decisions, and human judgement where individual circumstances matter most.
item.content:encoded:
Defaults are inevitable. 

For the past few years, we have been hearing about predictive analytics that can identify a borrower who is going to default before the default actually happens. 

Time and again, we have seen the limits of this idea. 

Defaults aren't a prediction problem that technology will eventually eliminate. Defaults are an uncertainty that lending produces, by design. What lenders need is not machinery that assumes this uncertainty can be removed, but machinery designed to operate effectively under it. 

You cannot predict at an individual borrower level who is going to default. You can, at best, predict, over a sufficiently large cohort of borrowers, what the default rate might be. 

The behaviour of large groups can be predicted statistically. The behaviour of a particular individual cannot. 

If you have one million borrowers, you can make remarkably good statements about what will happen to the portfolio. Narrow it to 100,000 borrowers in Karnataka, and you can still make useful predictions. Narrow it further by repayment history, geography, employment, credit score and other risk characteristics, and you can create increasingly meaningful cohorts. 

But as the cohorts get smaller, the certainty of those predictions starts decreasing. 

Eventually, you arrive at an individual borrower, say Ashok.Ashok's salary didn't arrive yesterday because his employer had a cash-flow problem. Your model cannot know that. It cannot know that unless you invade the privacy of Ashok and everyone he interacts with. Which you absolutely should not do. 

This is the fundamental limitation of trying to predict defaults at an individual level. 

For example, if we look at borrowers onboarded in Karnataka who have paid 60% of their EMIs on time and have a credit score of 650 or above, we may be able to say with reasonable confidence that 90% of them will repay on time in April. 

But we cannot tell you which 90%. 

And lenders have to operate with this uncertainty.

Borrowers do not fit into a neat Excel formula. Even if they did, you would not know all the variables that go into calculating it. 

Some of these variables are macro. 

In the western region, for instance, collections can soften during August and September around Ganesh Chaturthi. We also see periods where household cash flows come under pressure around the start of the school year, when families are managing school fees, admissions, books and other education-related expenses. 

This information is useful. 

It can tell us that collections might be lower during a particular period and help us anticipate how a portfolio could perform. 

But it still does not tell us who is going to miss their EMI. 

Then there are micro circumstances. 

A salary gets delayed. A business has a bad month. There is an unexpected expense. A school fee needs to be prioritised. Something happens in the family. Or someone simply forgets to maintain enough balance in their account. 

It is impossible for a lender to know every individual's circumstances at every point in time. This is why lending is ultimately a game of large numbers. 

Risk models can be extremely effective at estimating how a sufficiently large cohort will behave. But every individual in that cohort is a different person, going through a different set of circumstances. 

None of this is to say that predictive analytics is not useful. In fact, it is the opposite. 

Predictive analytics is a powerful tool when used for the problem it is actually capable of solving. It can tell you where a portfolio might end up. It can tell you where to focus effort. It can identify groups of borrowers that are more likely to need intervention than others. It can help lenders allocate their collection resources more intelligently and set realistic expectations for portfolio performance. 

The mistake is in assuming that this translates into certainty at the individual level. It doesn't. 

There will always be uncertainty at that level. And that means defaults will always exist. 

The more interesting opportunity for AI, therefore, is not to predict every default before it happens. It is to make lenders better at responding to defaults when they do happen.

When a borrower misses an EMI, the system should be able to help determine what happens next. Who needs an immediate intervention? Who is likely to self-cure? Which borrowers require a human conversation? What is the appropriate channel and timing? How should collection teams prioritise their limited resources? 

This is where predictive analytics, combined with AI-led decisioning and communication, can make a meaningful difference. 

The objective should not be to chase every borrower harder. It should be to make every intervention more relevant. 

That distinction matters, particularly as credit expands to millions of new borrowers across India. At that scale, collections cannot rely entirely on manual follow-ups, nor can it rely on the assumption that an algorithm will perfectly predict human behaviour. 

The future lies somewhere more practical: using data to understand portfolios, AI to prioritise decisions, and human judgement where individual circumstances matter most. 

Trying to predict every default before it happens is a game you cannot win. And it is a game you should not play. 

The real competitive advantage will come from building a system that accepts uncertainty, and is intelligent enough to deal with it.

The author is Co-founder & CTO, DPDzero, an AI-led debt collection platform.

item.title: 7 Books with twisted endings for psychological thriller Fans
item.description: Discover seven psychological thriller books with shocking twists, unreliable narrators and unexpected endings that will keep you guessing.
item.content:encoded:
Psychological thrillers are at their best when they make readers question everything they think they know.

A seemingly trustworthy character may be hiding a disturbing secret, an ordinary relationship may conceal years of manipulation, and a small detail introduced early in the story may completely change the meaning of everything that follows.

For fans of mind games, unreliable narrators and shocking revelations, a predictable ending can be disappointing. The real thrill comes from reaching the final pages and discovering that the story was never quite what it seemed.

If you enjoy books that keep you guessing until the very end, these seven psychological thrillers deserve a place on your reading list. Each offers a gripping mystery, unexpected turns or revelations that can change how you interpret the entire story.

7 Books with twisted endings for psychological thriller fans

1. The Silent Patient by Alex Michaelides

Alicia Berenson is a celebrated painter whose seemingly perfect life changes when her husband is murdered. After the killing, she stops speaking entirely. Years later, psychotherapist Theo Faber becomes determined to uncover what happened and understand her silence.

As Theo investigates Alicia's past, the distinction between truth, memory and obsession becomes increasingly difficult to navigate. The novel's final revelation encourages readers to reconsider the clues scattered throughout the story.

Why read it: Choose this if you love psychological suspense in which the narrator's perspective may be hiding more than it reveals. The ending is especially satisfying for readers who enjoy revisiting earlier chapters with a fresh understanding.

2. Gone Girl by Gillian Flynn

Nick Dunne becomes the prime suspect when his wife, Amy, disappears on their wedding anniversary. The evidence seems troubling, but the couple's marriage is more complicated than it initially appears.

Told through shifting perspectives, the novel gradually exposes the difference between public appearances and private realities. Gillian Flynn explores deception, control and the stories people construct to influence how others perceive them.

Why read it: This is an excellent choice for readers who enjoy morally complicated characters and stories that challenge their assumptions. Its revelations transform the mystery into a disturbing examination of marriage and manipulation.

3. Verity by Colleen Hoover

Lowen Ashleigh, a struggling writer, accepts a job completing a successful author's book series. While working at the author's home, she discovers an unpublished manuscript containing deeply disturbing accounts of the family's past.

As Lowen reads further, she begins questioning what she knows about Verity Crawford and the events surrounding her family. The story builds tension through competing versions of reality, leaving readers uncertain about whom they should believe.

Why read it: Read this if you enjoy disturbing secrets, morally ambiguous characters and endings that leave room for debate. The uncertainty surrounding the manuscript is a major part of the novel's appeal.

Also Read
10 Psychology books that change how you see daily habits

4. The Housemaid by Freida McFadden

Millie takes a job as a housemaid for a wealthy family, hoping for a fresh start. However, the seemingly comfortable household soon reveals unsettling dynamics, and her new position becomes more complicated than she expected.

As the story unfolds, the characters' motives become harder to read. What initially appears to be a straightforward domestic mystery develops into a tense story about power, secrets and survival.

Why read it: Its fast pace, short chapters and escalating revelations make it a strong pick for readers who want an addictive thriller they can finish over a weekend.

5. Rock Paper Scissors by Alice Feeney

Adam and Amelia travel to a remote location in Scotland in the hope of repairing their troubled marriage. Instead of bringing them closer, the trip creates an atmosphere of suspicion as long-buried secrets begin to surface.

Alternating perspectives and revelations about the couple's relationship gradually complicate the story. The isolated setting adds to the tension, while the narrative encourages readers to question how well spouses can truly know one another.

Why read it: This is a good choice if you enjoy relationship drama mixed with psychological suspense. It rewards readers who pay attention to small details and question what the characters choose to reveal.

6. The Wife Between Us by Greer Hendricks and Sarah Pekkanen

A complicated relationship involving a former wife, a new fiancée and a seemingly charming man sets the stage for this psychological thriller. At first, the situation appears to follow a familiar pattern of jealousy and romantic rivalry.

However, the narrative gradually challenges the assumptions readers make about the characters and their relationships. What appears straightforward becomes a more intricate story of deception, identity and control.

Why read it: Pick this up if you want a thriller that deliberately plays with your expectations. The changing picture of the characters is central to its suspense.

7. Behind Her Eyes by Sarah Pinborough

Louise becomes entangled in the lives of her new boss, David, and his wife, Adele, after a chance encounter leads to an unexpected connection. As she grows closer to both of them, she discovers that their marriage hides troubling secrets.

The story builds through suspicion, complicated loyalties and unanswered questions. Its final developments take the narrative in an unexpected direction, making it particularly suitable for readers who enjoy endings that challenge their understanding of the entire plot.

Why read it: Choose this for a particularly unconventional conclusion. If you enjoy psychological thrillers that push beyond familiar domestic mysteries, this one is worth considering.

Final thoughts

The best psychological thrillers do more than surprise readers with a final revelation. They build believable characters, plant subtle clues and create enough uncertainty to make every discovery feel significant.

Whether you prefer the calculated deception of Gone Girl, the unsettling atmosphere of Verity or the intricate mystery of The Silent Patient, these seven novels offer different approaches to suspense and misdirection.

If you are new to the genre, start with The Silent Patient. If you have already read the popular titles, try Rock Paper Scissors or The Wife Between Us for more relationship-driven mysteries.

item.title: CureBay raises Rs 100 Cr in Pre-Series C round led by IvyCap Ventures
item.description: CureBay said it will use the funds to expand its operations across India, strengthen its healthcare delivery network, and develop its technology and AI capabilities.
item.content:encoded:
Rural healthcare platform CureBay has raised Rs 100 crore in a Pre-Series C funding round led by IvyCap Ventures.

The round includes Rs 69 crore in equity from IvyCap Ventures and existing investors, along with over Rs 30 crore in debt from Trifecta Capital, Alteria Capital and VentureSoul Partners.

CureBay said it will use the funds to expand its operations across India, strengthen its healthcare delivery network, and develop its technology and AI capabilities. These include its Intelligence Layer, which is designed to support patient screening, health insights and clinical decision-making.

Founded in 2021 by Priyadarshi Mohapatra, Shobhan Mahapatra and Sanjay Swain, CureBay operates a technology-enabled rural healthcare network combining physical clinics with digital services. Its model includes IoT-enabled clinics, a network of Swasthya Mitras, a connected digital platform, AI-powered screening and risk alerts, a 24/7 command centre, and CureBay Kavach.

The company operates more than 250 technology-enabled clinics across seven states. It said it has served over 17 lakh patients and conducts more than 400 health camps each month.

“Rural Bharat doesn’t need another app; it needs a system that works end to end, from the Swasthya Mitra at the doorstep to the specialist in the city. This capital lets us take that operating system to more states and make our AI do the heavy lifting, so that every family gets the right care at the right time, close to home,” said Priyadarshi Mohapatra, Founder and CEO, CureBay.

“CureBay’s ability to combine technology with a strong on-ground healthcare network makes its model particularly compelling. As India works towards expanding access to quality healthcare across Bharat, we see significant potential in the company’s approach. We are excited to partner with CureBay as it scales its reach and continues to make quality healthcare more accessible to underserved communities across the country,” said Vikram Gupta, Founder and Managing Partner, IvyCap Ventures.

item.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (October 21, 2026)
item.description: YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Wednesday, October 21, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Companies from the startup ecosystem continue to show strong performance as listed firms, YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors.

Latest News

Eternal Q2 net profit rises 92% in FY27, revenue up 78%

Eternal, the parent company of Zomato and Blinkit, reported a 92.3% year-on-year (YoY) rise in net profit in the second quarter of FY27, while revenue grew 78% YoY. However, the company missed analysts’ estimates, which had projected a net profit of Rs 250 crore. Eternal’s net profit for the second quarter of FY27 stood at Rs 125 crore, compared with Rs 65 crore in the same period a year ago. Revenue rose to Rs 24,138 crore from Rs 13,590 crore in the corresponding quarter of the previous fiscal year.

Read more

Jio Platforms IPO oversubscribed in less than two hours led by QIBs

Jio Platforms’ initial public offering (IPO) was oversubscribed in the qualified institutional buyers (QIB) category within two hours of opening on Wednesday, signalling strong demand from institutional investors.

Read more

‘You are all born artists’: Prakash Belawadi on surviving the AI age

At TechSparks 2026, actor and theatre artist Prakash Belawadi reflected on AI’s impact on creativity and jobs, urging people to reconnect with their inner artist and find purpose beyond what technology can replace.

Read more

Funding news

Vectorial raises $3 million to scale AI-powered consumer research

Vectorial, an AI startup developing human behaviour simulation technology, has raised $3 million in a funding round led by SenseAI Ventures. The round also saw participation from Smilegate, Berkeley SkyDeck, Berkeley AI Research Lab, Dent Capital, Motus Ventures, SUM Ventures and strategic investors. The company has modelled more than 2.5 million people globally, including 500,000 in India, and conducted over 30,000 simulations. Its SAPIENS model uses demographic, psychological and behavioural data to predict how consumers may respond to digital products and experiences. Vectorial says its model is 30% more accurate than general-purpose large language models in predicting human behaviour. Its customers include boAt, GoodRx, Suki AI, Everkind and Concrete Software.

Onto raises $1 million to build AI-led travel platform

Bengaluru-based travel platform Onto has launched its services after raising $1 million in pre-seed funding. The round was led by Stargazer Fund and co-led by Singapore-based White Venture Capital. Founded by former Groww professionals Jagdeep Singh and Shubham Goyal, Onto aims to support travellers even after they complete a booking. Its first feature, Price Drop Refund, monitors hotel prices and automatically refunds eligible customers when the same hotel, room and dates become cheaper. The feature also covers eligible bookings made on other platforms, with refunds sent to the original payment method and updates shared through WhatsApp and app notifications. Onto said its app recorded more than 2,000 downloads before launch. The company will use the funds to expand operations, strengthen technology and develop AI-led travel products.

Enrission India Capital invests in freight-tech platform Raaho

Japan-based Enrission India Capital has invested in Raaho, a Gurugram-based digital freight platform, although the round size was not disclosed. Founded in 2017, Raaho connects logistics companies with truck owners through digital matching, verification and settlement, replacing parts of the traditional offline broker model. The company reported year-on-year growth of about 50%, with trip volumes rising around 75%, and recorded its first full year of profitability in FY26. It currently operates in 20 cities. The investment will support expansion to 25 cities, entry into the open-truck category and deeper use of artificial intelligence in load matching, pricing, document processing and customer interactions. Raaho combines technology with on-ground operations to serve India’s fragmented trucking market, where many operators own fewer than 10 trucks.

GrowthCap Ventures backs autonomous aircraft startup LogiXair

GrowthCap Ventures has invested in Hyderabad-based deep-tech company LogiXair, which is developing autonomous hybrid-electric vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) aircraft for cargo logistics. Founded by Bhanu Teja Chidura and Pulla Kapil, the startup is targeting short-haul cargo movement of up to 600 km between metros, industrial hubs and smaller cities without conventional runways. Its L560 aircraft is designed to carry up to 300 kg. LogiXair says it has validated a hybrid-electric powertrain, flight-tested sub-scale prototypes and developed six intellectual-property assets at Technology Readiness Level 6. The company also works with DRDO and aerospace and defence original equipment manufacturers. The investment will fund engineering development, technology validation and commercialisation, while the company explores partnerships across logistics, industrial and strategic sectors and prepares for potential international markets.

Other news

Vultr to deploy 20 MW AMD AI supercluster in Chennai

Cloud infrastructure provider Vultr plans to deploy AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs in a new 20-megawatt supercluster in Chennai. The company said the facility will be India’s largest AMD Instinct deployment and one of its two largest AI infrastructure deployments globally. Each GPU offers 288GB of HBM3E memory and 8TB per second of memory bandwidth. The supercluster is intended to support AI labs, foundation-model developers, startups, enterprises and academic institutions with workloads including model training, fine-tuning and inference. Vultr said locally available computing capacity can help organisations meet data-residency, sovereignty and latency requirements. The deployment will use AMD’s ROCm open software ecosystem, giving developers access to AI frameworks, libraries and models. Vultr also plans further global capacity expansion in 2027 using next-generation AMD infrastructure.

Girikon.AI develops Koyal voice AI model

Technology company Girikon.AI has developed Koyal, a voice AI model designed to support more natural and adaptable voice interactions across languages and applications. The company said the model focuses on aspects such as pronunciation, tone, language nuances and conversational context, which can influence how people experience voice-based technology. The development comes as enterprises explore conversational AI for customer service, sales, support and other business functions. Girikon.AI said voice interfaces that accommodate regional language preferences and communication styles could make digital services easier to access in India’s linguistically diverse market.

Agrograde deploys AI-powered arecanut sorting system in Mangaluru

Physical AI startup Agrograde has deployed what it describes as India’s first AI-powered optical sorting system developed specifically for arecanut. The first commercial installation is at Vikas Traders in Mangaluru, Karnataka. The system can process about one tonne an hour, enabling the facility to handle close to eight tonnes daily. Using computer vision, it captures multiple images of each nut, identifies visible defects and separates rejected material from accepted produce. Agrograde said the model’s sorting accuracy improved from around 75% at commissioning to approximately 89% as it incorporated commercial operating data. The system also generates quality summaries covering size distribution, defects and packed quantities.

OpenAI and Karmayogi Bharat sign MoU

Karmayogi Bharat and OpenAI have signed a memorandum of understanding to strengthen AI capacity development across India’s civil services. Under the collaboration, approved OpenAI Academy learning resources will be made available through the iGOT Karmayogi platform, which supports training for government personnel at the Centre and in the states. OpenAI will provide the approved content, while Karmayogi Bharat will coordinate access, learner engagement and engagement with relevant government departments.

The initiative aims to help civil servants build practical AI skills for everyday work and public-service delivery. Chhavi Bhardwaj, CEO of Karmayogi Bharat, said the collaboration would support responsible and confident use of AI. OpenAI India’s Pragya Misra noted that more than 1.7 crore government employees are registered on iGOT Karmayogi, offering a route to build AI capabilities at scale.

Motorica begins local production of bionic hand prostheses in India

Russian medical technology company Motorica has started local production of its Indy Hand bionic prosthesis at its Indian partner’s facility in Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh. The initiative involves transferring manufacturing technology, training local staff and introducing production and quality-control processes. Motorica said several dozen prostheses have already been manufactured, with some fitted to users. Indy Hand is a myoelectric forearm prosthesis for people with upper-limb amputations or congenital limb differences. It weighs 520 grams, supports multiple grip patterns and can lift loads of up to 10 kg. Local production is expected to reduce costs through domestic component sourcing and lower logistics expenses, while improving service responsiveness. Motorica has operated in India since 2021 and has established a network of more than 60 partner clinics. It plans to expand local production and introduce additional products.

VORAN and Polish firm explore gyroplane technology partnership

India’s VORAN Private Limited and Poland-based W&S Innovation – Aviation Artur Trendak have signed a memorandum of understanding to explore collaboration in gyroplane aviation and potential light-aircraft manufacturing in India. Initial areas of interest include the X2 advanced gyroplane and AAT TAIFUN, alongside other products the companies may agree on. The proposed collaboration could cover market development, design, technical know-how, support, product development, aircraft sales, pilot training, maintenance and technical-skills development. Any technology transfer or intellectual-property licensing would require separate agreements. The X2 features retractable landing gear, a shock-absorbing landing system, upward-opening electric doors and avionics including GPS navigation and liquid-crystal displays. VORAN said the partnership is part of its effort to connect international aviation expertise with Indian talent and develop capabilities in the country’s light-aviation sector.

KickSky opens applications for third space-tech accelerator cohort

KickSky Space Lab has opened applications for the third cohort of its accelerator for space-technology startups, with the programme expected to begin on December 1, 2026. The accelerator plans to select five to six companies. Founded in 2023 by deep-tech investors Riceberg Ventures, E2MC Ventures and Aniara Space, KickSky has supported 11 startups across its first two cohorts. Six graduates have secured funding or exited, according to the organisation. The six-month programme combines four months of active acceleration with two months of post-programme support. Selected startups will receive a $10,000 stipend, customised technical and business mentorship, commercialisation support and introductions to investors, customers and industry partners. KickSky is also developing partnerships to help startups with legal, regulatory, banking, testing and launch-related requirements. In June 2026, Ideabaaz acquired a 25% strategic stake in KickSky.

YatriKart and MMG Group plan 1,000 Quick Stop stores

Convenience retail company YatriKart has announced a ₹120 crore partnership with MMG Group to establish 1,000 Quick Stop stores across India over five years. Under the Franchise Invested, Company Operated model, MMG will fund store infrastructure and capital expenditure, while YatriKart will manage operating costs, technology, supply chain, staffing and daily operations. The first phase targets 100 stores in Delhi NCR, with locations planned at fuel stations, highways, bus stands and other transit hubs. YatriKart currently operates more than 80 stores across eight cities, selling coffee, food, beverages and everyday essentials. The company also plans to launch a consumer app that will let customers find stores along their routes, order ahead and receive products at participating locations. The 1,000-store plan supports YatriKart’s broader ambition to build a 5,000-store network nationwide.

boAt expands into Sri Lanka and Bhutan

Consumer technology brand boAt has expanded into Sri Lanka and Bhutan as it seeks to grow its international business beyond India. The company said international revenue more than doubled in FY26, providing early momentum for its overseas strategy. The new markets add to its presence across Southeast Asia and the Gulf Cooperation Council region. boAt is entering Sri Lanka and Bhutan with products spanning personal audio, smartwatches and charging solutions, and plans to adapt its portfolio according to local consumer preferences and market response. The expansion forms part of its “boAt 2.0” strategy, which includes entering new consumer-technology categories while building on its audio business. The company said wearables turned profitable in FY26 and charging products contributed to growth in profit beyond audio. Its India-based boAt Labs research and development centre has more than 100 engineers.

Azul releases security-only updates addressing 53 OpenJDK vulnerabilities

Enterprise Java provider Azul has released October Security-only, Stability-first updates for Azul Core to address all 53 vulnerabilities disclosed in the latest quarterly OpenJDK update. The company said the update contains security fixes without new features or unrelated changes, reducing the risk of software regressions during urgent patching. Azul described the vulnerability count as the highest in a single OpenJDK update in well over a decade and seven times the two-year quarterly average. It warned that AI tools are helping researchers uncover long-standing software flaws and enabling attackers to exploit vulnerabilities more quickly, while enterprise patch cycles can take weeks. Azul said its security-only updates are designed for immediate production deployment and are available for supported long-term Java releases. It also provides backported security fixes for organisations still running Java 6 and Java 7.

Fynd enters manufacturing technology with AI-powered Forge platform

Fynd, an AI-native unified commerce technology company, has entered the manufacturing technology segment with the launch of Fynd Forge, an AI-enabled manufacturing execution system. The platform is already operational at electronics manufacturer NeoLync’s facility in Tirupati, Andhra Pradesh. Forge manages more than 100 stations and nearly 90 process stages, with 160 operators using the system concurrently during each shift. It supports manufacturing processes ranging from component receipt and assembly to testing, packing and dispatch. Its AI assistant enables teams to analyse production and quality data, identify stalled work orders, investigate defects and build workflows using natural-language commands. The platform also enforces quality checks and maintains product traceability. The launch marks Fynd’s expansion beyond retail and commerce into manufacturing operations.

ISS India opens Bengaluru office to strengthen UK-India business ties

UK-based ISS India Ltd. has opened an office in Bengaluru to help businesses, particularly micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), access and expand in the Indian and British markets. The inauguration was attended by Kim McGuinness, Chair of The Great North Trade Mission to India, alongside British Deputy High Commission officials, entrepreneurs and investors. The company also announced a three-day roadshow across key business hubs in North and Northeast England in late November 2026 for an Indian business and startup delegation. ISS India aims to support market entry, identify partners and distributors, and connect businesses with investment opportunities, universities and supply chains. Its leadership said the Bengaluru office would facilitate bilateral trade and collaboration following the UK-India trade agreement, with plans to expand into other Indian cities as demand grows.

LTM launches BlueVerse ValueMesh for enterprise AI execution

LTM has launched BlueVerse ValueMesh, an AI execution fabric designed to help enterprises scale artificial intelligence across the Oracle transformation lifecycle, from strategy and implementation to operations and continuous innovation. The offering brings together AI-enabled delivery, intelligent automation, AI agents, managed services, business processes, industry solutions, data and governance. It is organised around three layers: Enterprise AI for transformation, software engineering, testing and cloud operations; Business AI for functions such as finance, supply chain, human resources and customer experience; and Industrial AI for assets, field operations and sector-specific workflows. LTM’s four-stage framework—Sense, Shape, Stand Up and Sustain—is intended to help organisations identify AI opportunities, design solutions, deploy them and improve performance continuously. The company said the platform aims to move enterprises beyond isolated pilots towards scalable adoption, faster time-to-value and measurable business outcomes across their Oracle environments.

Federal Bank appoints Cognizant India chief Rajesh Varrier as independent director

Federal Bank has appointed Rajesh Varrier, chairman and managing director of Cognizant India, as an independent director on its board for a three-year term. The appointment, as an additional non-executive independent director, took effect on October 16, 2026, according to a regulatory filing by the private-sector lender. The bank said Varrier is not related to any of its directors. In his role at Cognizant India, Varrier provides regional leadership for the company’s India leadership council and India-based workforce, with a focus on transformation programmes and executing its growth plans across the country. The appointment brings technology-services leadership experience to Federal Bank’s board. The filing did not provide further details about Varrier’s specific responsibilities on the board or any committee assignments arising from the appointment.

NuvoRetail launches AI-powered Amazon listing optimisation tool

E-commerce marketing and analytics agency NuvoRetail has launched Content Studio by enlytical.ai, an AI-powered solution to analyse, optimise and publish Amazon product listings. It scores product pages out of 100, examines titles, descriptions, images and brand content, and identifies gaps against competitors. NuvoRetail said the solution is designed to make listing optimisation faster and more scalable, particularly for brands managing large catalogues during high-demand shopping periods.

item.title: eMudhra to exit global website security certificate business
item.description: The move follows scrutiny over weak cryptographic keys, with eMudhra citing rising compliance costs and declining returns from a business that contributes just 1% of its revenue.
item.content:encoded:
Bengaluru-based digital trust company eMudhra has decided to exit its global SSL/TLS certificate business following a security incident involving weak cryptographic keys that prompted action from Google and Mozilla. In a regulatory filing on Thursday, the company said its board had decided to voluntarily withdraw from the business, citing rising compliance costs, increasing data sovereignty requirements and diminishing commercial returns. The decision follows the discovery of eight intermediate certificate authority keys linked to eMudhra that were found to be dangerously weak, potentially allowing attackers to impersonate legitimate websites. The keys were generated in April 2025, but the weakness remained undetected for about 18 months. Google and Mozilla subsequently moved to block the affected certificates to protect users. eMudhra Chairman V Srinivasan said the company had revoked the affected certificate authorities within 14 hours of discovering the incident and promptly disclosed the issue.

The company maintained that its infrastructure had not been compromised, no data had been breached and none of the affected intermediate authorities had issued end-user certificates.

Global SSL/TLS certificates, which help authenticate websites and secure online communications, contribute approximately 1% of eMudhra's global revenue.

Srinivasan said increasing data sovereignty and compliance requirements had made the business more complex and expensive to operate. Competition from large providers offering SSL/TLS certificates free of cost had also reduced its commercial potential and return on investment.

"The level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS's place in our business," Srinivasan said.

He added that the board, following detailed deliberations, had concluded that withdrawing from the global SSL/TLS business was the right decision for the company and its shareholders.

eMudhra said it would now sharpen its focus on core enterprise solutions and digital trust services outside the SSL/TLS segment.

What happens to existing customers?

The company said its G1 RSA root certificates would continue to serve customers during the transition as it works with browser programmes and customers to facilitate the withdrawal.

It will reach out to affected customers and arrange replacement certificates free of cost through partners.

Revocation and certificate status services will continue until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced.

eMudhra also committed to fulfilling its remaining obligations to browser root programmes, including submitting a full root-cause report on the incident. It has not specified a timeline for completing the exit.

Other operations unaffected

The company clarified that its global SSL/TLS infrastructure operates separately from its other businesses, including its Indian digital signature certificate (DSC) and eSign services. Its enterprise public key infrastructure platforms, including emCA and CertiNext, emSigner eSignature Suite and identity and authentication solutions such as SecurePass and emAS, will also continue operating normally. The incident has drawn scrutiny from global browser providers and Indian authorities. Google's Chrome Security team had warned that the weak keys could allow attackers to forge trusted HTTPS certificates, while Mozilla blocked the affected certificates in Firefox.

India's Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) also issued an advisory on October 21, flagging the risks associated with the compromised certificate keys.

eMudhra, which provides digital identity, trust and security solutions across more than 35 countries, said the decision would allow it to concentrate resources on its broader enterprise technology portfolio.

item.title: Celebrities don't sell, the product does: Ananth Narayanan on what makes a D2C brand last
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, the BRND.ME founder says the growth-hack era is over and the brands that survive will be built on product love, cash flows and global ambition.
item.content:encoded:
The froth has gone out of D2C, and brands that want to last will have to earn it slowly. That was the message from Ananth Narayanan, Founder and CEO of BRND.ME, at the 17th edition of YourStory's TechSparks.

In a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, Narayanan said the shift towards profitable businesses began two to three years ago. "Without product-market fit, just scaling, which a lot of D2C brands used to do, I don't think is valued anymore," he said. "You need real cash flows, you need real product love, which is very hard."

There is no shortcut, he added, "I don't think there is a get-rich-quick on brand building." In his experience a brand takes seven to 15 years to earn real loyalty and cohorts that last five or ten years. Patient capital is becoming easier to find, he said, through FMCG majors such as Unilever and P&G buying D2C brands, and through a coming wave of IPOs. Founders can help themselves by being frugal. "Most of the large FMCG businesses never took any money. Is it possible for D2C to do the same? I think the answer is yes. It's hard. It's very unsexy."

Think global from day one

Narayanan believes India's next big brands will be built for overseas shoppers. The old barriers of consumer understanding and distribution are easing, he said, with Amazon Global Selling for reach and AI agents trained on Reddit threads and Amazon reviews to stand in for foreign consumers. BRND.ME, which earns more than half its revenue outside India, uses such agents in product development.

His example was Majestic Pure, the group's aromatherapy brand. India is one of the world's top essential-oil producers, and the two biggest aromatherapy brands, doTERRA and Young Living, both American, source over 30% of their production here. Majestic Pure sells comparable products at around $25 against their $65. "It is not the same packaging," he said. "There is a story that you have to learn to tell to command the price premium."

His tip for founders: look at what India exports in bulk, and ask whether a brand can be built on top of it. He named categories like pet care and health and wellness.

Focus, R&D and packaging

BRND.ME has cut down its portfolio to MyFitness, Majestic Pure, Botanic Heart and Party Props. "Our overall business is larger, but the number of brands that we have is smaller," he said. He also called for more real R&D from Indian FMCG firms, citing Botanic Heart's two-year push on efficacy testing so that its claims hold up in the US.

On packaging, he admitted the company still hires a US agency for design. "Packaging is marketing," he said. "You're competing with the Korean brand, the European brand."

"The celebrity may add recall, but the product sells"

On celebrity-led brands, Narayanan was blunt. "A face can give you initial momentum, but I don't think it can get you repeat consumers." Paying an ambassador for a campaign is fine if the return on spend justifies it, he said. Making a celebrity a partner is a different matter, and works only if the star fits the brand and a seasoned business person makes the product, marketing and pricing calls. Otherwise, "you think the celebrity sells, but reality is the product sells." Sharma called it the headline of the session.

Brands that mislead consumers, he said, do not last. "Maybe you can fool consumers once, but I don't think you can fool them again." His advice was to keep 8 to 20% of revenue coming from a brand's own channel, since quick commerce and marketplaces give little feedback, and to be honest about reviews and ratings.

Quick commerce and the cash-flow game

Quick commerce is here to stay, Narayanan said, and works best where speed changes the purchase, as with Party Props. For an FMCG item bought once or twice a month, shelf space is tight and the platforms will take more of the value. He rejected the idea of a monopoly. "There is no monopolistic world in India. If you can compete here, you can compete globally."

He does not judge founders who build to sell, but said that "eventually all valuation games have to be cash flow games, because the only real exit eventually is an IPO." His own aim is a long game. His parting advice to founders was to build with heart: "Build products that you love. Otherwise you are becoming a bit of a machine that churns out unit economics."

Brand India and early-stage funding

Asked how he would pitch India as a brand, Narayanan said it stands for talent today and should now move on to culture, from yoga and Ayurveda to mindfulness. "Why can't we make the Indian way of living the most important thing in the digital age?"

Answering an audience member who said pre-seed D2C funding is hard to come by, he disagreed. "There is a lot of money available if you have a good idea for a consumer brand. In fact, the later stage is much harder. Early stage, it's an idea, and most people like ideas."

item.title: TravClan raises $5M from Flipkart, others
item.description: TravClan said it will use the funds to expand its global supply network, enhance its technology and AI capabilities, and strengthen destination operations across key international markets.
item.content:encoded:
TravClan, a traveltech startup, has raised $5 million in funding from Flipkart and August One, along with debt financing from Trifecta Capital.

The startup said it will use the funds to expand its global supply network, enhance its technology and AI capabilities, and strengthen destination operations across key international markets.

TravClan provides a technology platform that integrates supply, technology and fulfilment infrastructure for travel businesses. Its platform supports various functions, including pricing, itinerary creation, bookings, payments, fulfilment, customer communication and on-ground support.

The startup helps travel businesses sell and fulfil bookings for flights, hotels, activities and international holiday packages.

“Our ambition is to make TravClan the infrastructure that any travel business can build on instead of having to recreate the entire travel stack itself. This capital allows us to invest aggressively behind that opportunity,” said TravClan co-founder & CEO Arun Bagaria.

According to TravClan, it enables travel agents to plan, price and rebuild complex international itineraries in a shorter period of time. It also brings global inventory, pricing, booking, AI-powered workflows and destination fulfillment into one platform.

TravClan claims more than 15,000 travel agents across India use their platform to book flights, hotels, activities and destination services processing more than $100 million in annual travel sales. Around 40% of the company’s business now originates from Tier II and Tier III cities, reflecting the growing demand for international travel beyond India’s largest metros.

“TravClan has built a capital efficient model by owning supply rather than buying demand, and distributing through agents in underserved markets,” said Sahil Kukreja, Vice President, Trifecta Capital.

“We backed them when owning supply looked like the slow way to build. It has compounded in two ways — better prices, and a trip that actually works when something goes wrong. In travel, whoever owns the supply owns the economics,” said Rajul Garg, Founder & Managing Partner, Leo Capital.

item.title: eMudhra faces scrutiny after weak certificate keys raise web security concerns
item.description: Eight weak intermediate certificate keys have prompted browser safeguards and questions over eMudhra’s controls, although the company said customer data and Indian eSign services remain unaffected.
item.content:encoded:
Eight intermediate certificate authority keys linked to eMudhra’s global website-security business were found to be dangerously weak, raising concerns about the systems that browsers use to establish trust online.

The flaw could have enabled attackers to create fraudulent HTTPS certificates and impersonate legitimate websites. The keys were generated on April 30, 2025, but the weakness remained undetected for about 18 months, according to eMudhra’s statement on October 21, 2026.

A certificate authority (CA) verifies identities and issues digital certificates. Intermediate authorities operate under a root certificate trusted by browsers and operating systems.

eMudhra said a key-wrap/unwrap step during its key-generation procedure produced a second, weak set of keys, which were subsequently published to browser root stores. Although the company added its root private key was not compromised, browser operators have withdrawn trust from the associated emSign ECC Root CA - G3 as a precaution.

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has emphasised the distinction between eMudhra’s domestic digital-signature business and its international website-security operations. The ministry said the latter operates under a global trust framework and is subject to independent audits, including WebTrust audits conducted by BDO International Limited. It also stated, “The reported security incident pertains to this only. MeitY is not involved in its audit.” A special team has been constituted to investigate the matter, according to a report by The Indian Express.

Google’s Chrome Security team warned that the flaw was “enabling anyone to forge trusted HTTPS certificates to impersonate any website against clients that have not yet removed trust in those CAs.” Google blocked the affected keys and plans to remove the parent root from Chrome’s trust store from October 27, Pacific time. Some legitimate websites using certificates under that root may consequently stop functioning in Chrome.

Mozilla, meanwhile, blocked the affected certificates in Firefox within three hours of receiving the report and released software updates to extend protection to users who might not receive automatic safeguards.

MeitY has described the impact on Indian websites and applications as very limited and brief. However, CERT-In has separately warned that removing the associated root certificate from browser and application trust stores may cause legitimate certificates to become untrusted, potentially disrupting affected websites and services.

eMudhra said none of the eight affected intermediate authorities issued end-user certificates, its infrastructure was not compromised and no data was breached. It identifies one affected customer ecosystem in the United States, where certificates are being replaced.

The company stated its Indian digital-signature and eSign services, which operate on separate infrastructure, remain unaffected. It acknowledged uncertainty over the cause, noting, “We have not yet confirmed the exact root cause. We will publish it in full once our investigation is complete.”

The incident highlights a wider challenge for the digital-trust industry. Encryption can protect communications, but only when the certificates establishing a website’s identity are reliable. Browser companies therefore maintain their own trusted certificate lists and can revoke acceptance when a provider’s controls fail.

Public Certificate Transparency logs also help detect suspicious certificate issuance. The uncomfortable question for eMudhra is how a weakness of this significance escaped detection through two audit cycles. 

The company said it is reviewing its key-generation procedures and offering enterprise customers certificates from an additional certificate authority to reduce dependence on a single trust chain.

item.title: Finance influencer V Harish dies by suicide; father alleges cyberbullying
item.description: The family has accused a venture studio CEO of online harassment. The CEO denies the allegation and says he had questioned Harish's financial regulatory credentials.
item.content:encoded:
(Trigger warning: Story mentions suicide)

V Harish, a financial influencer with over a million followers, has died by suicide at a rented villa near Chennai. His father has alleged that Harish was reportedly “targeted” by Jason Samuel, the CEO of venture studio Zemuria Inc. Harish’s Instagram account was disabled by Meta following allegations made by Samuel, after which he began posting videos on a new handle. Samuel has denied the cyberbullying allegations.

Samuel took to X on Tuesday and wrote, “I am deeply saddened, heavily grieving, shocked and frozen at what has happened and I mourn the loss of life.” 

“I have not cyber-bullied him. I pointed out his lack of license and authority, misrepresentation of license and fraud on SEBI and AMFI where he has not got SEBI RIA for his work and misrepresented that he had an AMFI license when he got the ARN only recently. i.e., his illegal activity.”

He added, “I literally asked him in the video to come back and do this with a proper SEBI license. I never intended or expected this drastic measure to happen and I mourn the loss.”

item.title: Eternal to pick 4.4% stake in Mygate following divestment of digital ad business
item.description: Eternal will divest its stake in AdOnMo to acquire stake in Mygate through a share-swap deal, combining community management services with a network of digital advertising screens.
item.content:encoded:
Eternal, the parent company of Blinkit and Zomato, will acquire a 4.4% stake in Mygate through a share-swap agreement as it divests its stake in outdoor digital advertising business AdOnMo.

In a disclosure to the stock exchanges, Eternal said it will transfer 11,214 Series B compulsorily convertible preference shares and 10 equity shares in AdOnMo Private Limited to Mygate. In exchange, Eternal will acquire 1,84,091 Series C1 compulsorily convertible preference shares and 164 equity shares in Mygate.

Founded in 2016, AdOnMo operates a cloud-connected network of digital screens across residential communities, commercial buildings, tech parks and public spaces, including supermarkets, malls and metro stations. Eternal invested Rs 112 crore in the company in January 2022. AdOnMo operates across 27 cities, with a presence in more than 7,000 gated communities and over 200 million sq. ft. of office space.

According to Mygate, the transaction will expand its offerings as a community management platform. Mygate has a presence in 30,000 residential communities, while AdOnMo brings a network of 55,000 connected digital screens.

Sandeep Bommireddi and Sravanth Gajula, Founders of AdOnMo, will be joining Mygate’s board as co-founders.

“Communities gain an integrated digital screen infrastructure to communicate critical updates and information effortlessly with residents—all while we continue to uphold the trust and privacy our community residents expect from us," said Mygate co-founder & CEO Abhishek Kumar.

"AdOnMo was founded with a vision that ambient advertising could become as intelligent, measurable and technology driven as digital advertising at scale," said Sandeep Bommireddi and Sravanth Gajula, Co-founders, AdOnMo. "Joining hands with Mygate allows us to accelerate this vision and create greater value for RWAs, residents, developers and brands alike."

item.title: Chapter Home raises Rs 63 Cr in a mix of equity and debt
item.description: Chapter Home said it will use the funding for product development, expansion into newer categories, and investment into technology .
item.content:encoded:
Chapter Home, a home and kitchen consumer brand, has raised Rs 63 crore through a mix of equity and debt at a valuation of nearly Rs 1,000 crore. The funding round saw participation from Bessemer Venture Partners, Stride Ventures, influencer Tanmay Bhat, and select family offices.

According to a statement, the company will use the capital to strengthen product development, expand into new categories, invest in technology and brand building, and scale its omnichannel distribution network, including physical touchpoints that are currently being developed.

Founded in 2025 by Nitin Chugh, Akarsh Bharadwaj, Shrey Mittal, Dhiraj Jain and Dheeraj Goyal, Chapter Home is an omnichannel platform focused on building consumer brands across the home and kitchen segment. Its product portfolio spans bed and table linen, cookware, home décor, and small kitchen appliances. The founders were part of the founding and leadership teams at PharmEasy.

The company entered the home furnishings market with HOKIPO, an online brand offering home furnishing products.

“Consumers are increasingly looking for better-designed products, trusted quality, strong functionality and a superior overall experience—online and in store—and we see a meaningful opportunity to build for those needs. That is why we are building focused brands for each category across Home & Kitchen,” said Nitin Chugh, Co-founder of Chapter Home.

According to Chapter Home, it leverages AI across the business - from cataloguing and content to demand forecasting, product assortment, customer targeting and retention; Thus, enabling each brand to launch faster and at lower cost.

Chapter Home aims to combine strong product development, sourcing and brand building with omnichannel distribution across marketplaces & quick commerce platforms, its own D2C channel and offline retail.

“Chapter Home's approach of building a focused brand for each part of the home on a shared technology, sourcing and distribution backbone fits how this market actually works,” said Anant Vidur Puri, Partner Bessemer Venture Partners.

item.title: Startup news and updates: Daily roundup (October22, 2026)
item.description: YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Thursday, October 22, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors.

Featured stories

Meet the ‘Flower Lady of Manipur’ 

Chokhone Krichena, founder of Manipur-based social enterprise Dianthe, is helping over 300 women farmers turn their love of flowers into income. Founded in 2021, Dianthe works with women in Mao, Senapati district, to source locally grown flowers, preserve them through natural drying techniques, and sell them to customers across India. What began during the Covid-19 pandemic as an effort to find buyers for surplus flowers has grown into a business supplying home décor products to customers in 20 states.

Read more

Funding news

Karta AI raises $3 million to scale voice AI for financial services

Karta AI, a voice AI platform that automates inbound customer operations for banks, financial services and insurance companies, has raised $3 million in a funding round led by PeerCapital and Cedar Hill Capital. Wyser VC, CDM Capital and Seedstars also participated. The company says it handles around two million customer conversations every month across more than 25 languages and is already deployed with financial institutions.

The platform uses AI agents to understand customer requests and resolve issues such as failed payments, blocked cards, loan queries and insurance claims by coordinating actions across enterprise systems. Unlike conventional voice bots that primarily answer questions, Karta AI aims to complete customer service workflows autonomously, escalating cases to human agents when needed. Its technology also learns from past interactions to improve resolution over time.

CureBay raises Rs 100 crore in Pre-Series C round 

Rural healthcare platform CureBay has raised Rs 100 crore in a Pre-Series C funding round led by IvyCap Ventures. The round includes Rs 69 crore in equity from IvyCap Ventures and existing investors, along with over Rs 30 crore in debt from Trifecta Capital, Alteria Capital and VentureSoul Partners.

Founded in 2021 by Priyadarshi Mohapatra, Shobhan Mahapatra and Sanjay Swain, CureBay operates over 250 technology-enabled clinics across seven states. The company will use the funds to expand its operations, strengthen its healthcare delivery network and develop its technology and AI capabilities, including tools for patient screening, health insights and clinical decision-making. CureBay says it has served over 17 lakh patients and conducts more than 400 health camps every month.

Read more

Other news

Uroionpro Transit, Mastercard partner to simplify transit payments

Uroionpro Transit is expanding its partnership with Mastercard to help public transport agencies and government authorities across North America modernise transit payment systems and improve passenger experience. The collaboration focuses on making contactless payment solutions easier to assess, procure and deploy across public transportation networks.

The partnership will support transit agencies through practical procurement frameworks, repeatable implementation methods and deployment models that can be adapted to local operational and policy requirements. The aim is to reduce the complexity of introducing contactless payments while enabling secure, seamless and convenient transactions for passengers.

Maasi launches on-demand nanny platform in Bengaluru

Maasi, a childcare platform offering trained, background-verified nannies on demand and through subscription plans, has launched in Bengaluru. During its invite-only beta, the platform served 1,200 families and built a waitlist of over 5,000 parents. Instant Nanny visits start at Rs 660, while subscription plans begin at Rs 15,660 a month.

Founded by Gargi Pandey, Aashu Manchali and Reshov Roy, Maasi offers short-notice childcare and part-time, full-time, live-in, governess and postpartum care. The startup aims to address the shortage of reliable childcare, which can force parents, particularly women, to step away from their careers. Its caregivers undergo background verification and training, with replacement support if a caregiver leaves

Pine Labs partners WEBXPAY to enable UPI payments in Sri Lanka

Pine Labs has partnered with Sri Lankan payment aggregator WEBXPAY to enable Indian payment methods across its merchant network in Sri Lanka. The collaboration is the country's first Payment Aggregator-to-Payment Aggregator partnership under India’s RBI-authorised PA-CB framework.

Through the partnership, merchants can accept UPI, UPI AutoPay, cards from major Indian issuers, net banking across more than 100 banks, EMI conversions and Credit on UPI. The solution offers T+1 settlement and integrates with existing merchant systems, enabling Indian travellers to pay in Sri Lanka using familiar methods.

Vultr announces Chennai cloud data centre region with 20 MW AI supercluster

Cloud infrastructure provider Vultr has announced Chennai as its 34th global cloud data centre region, featuring an AI supercluster powered by AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, starting at 20 MW. The facility aims to give Indian enterprises and developers access to high-performance computing infrastructure closer to where they build and deploy AI applications.

Vultr plans to expand the supercluster in 2027 with next-generation AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs and AMD Helios rack-scale technology. The company said the infrastructure will help enterprises scale AI projects from pilots to production while offering greater control over workloads through an open software foundation.

Binny Bansal-backed ShopOS launches AI creative platform Sloosh

ShopOS, a Bengaluru-based AI company backed by Flipkart co-founder Binny Bansal’s 3STATE Ventures, has launched Sloosh.ai, an AI creative platform that converts ideas, photos and videos into product imagery, visual scenes, reels and creator-style clips. The platform is now available globally, giving creators and businesses access to ShopOS’ creative engine.

ShopOS has raised $20 million and uses AI agents, reusable workflows and human experts to produce content for global and Indian brands. With Sloosh, the company aims to make AI-powered creative production more accessible and lower-cost for agency teams, brands, founders, small businesses, and independent creators.

Sirona launches ‘Unpause Menopause’ campaign to break stigma

Women’s period care and wellness brand Sirona has launched ‘Unpause Menopause’, a campaign aimed at breaking the silence around menopause and challenging the stigma and ageism associated with this stage of women’s health. Built around the message “Cut the noise. Start the conversation,” the initiative encourages women to speak openly about their experiences without embarrassment.

The campaign highlights lesser-discussed menopause symptoms, including joint aches, itchy ears, dizziness, heart palpitations, changes in body odour, and dry eyes. While conversations around periods and reproductive health have gained visibility, menopause often remains a private struggle.

Beginning October 18, the brand has mobilised some of India's most influential voices to speak openly about menopause, their experiences, their symptoms, and why the silence has gone on too long. On October 21, Sirona released the Unpause Menopause brand film alongside a curated series of expert conversations, bringing together doctors, specialists and women who have lived through this transition to address the questions most women have never had the space to ask. The film and expert series are available on Sirona's YouTube channel and Instagram page.

In a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, Narayanan said, without product-market fit, merely scaling, which a lot of D2C brands used to do, is not valued anymore. “You need real cash flows, you need real product love, which is very hard,” he said.

  • A celebrity may add recall to a brand, but it’s the product that sells, said Narayanan. “A face can give you initial momentum, but I don’t think it can get you repeat consumers.”
  • He advised founders to build with heart. “Build products that you love. Otherwise you are becoming a bit of a machine that churns out unit economics.”
  • On India as a brand, Narayanan said the country stands for talent and should now move on to culture, from yoga and Ayurveda to mindfulness. “Why can’t we make the Indian way of living the most important thing in the digital age?”

item.title: Jio Platforms IPO draws strong demand within hours; Eternal's Q2 net profit rises 92%
item.description: The qualified institutional investors showed strong interest for the IPO of Jio Platforms with subscription crossing 4x.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

Jio Platforms’ blockbuster IPO sets the tone for a week in which investor confidence, technology ambitions, and digital trust take centre stage. The Rs 30,213-crore issue drew strong demand from qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) within two hours of opening on Wednesday, with the institutional portion subscribed nearly five times. Jio’s ambitions span telecom, artificial intelligence (AI), cloud and digital services, although retail and non-institutional investor participation remained comparatively muted.

The AI race is also becoming more competitive. OpenAI is expanding beyond its longstanding dependence on Microsoft by bringing its models to Google Cloud, signalling a more diversified approach to computing infrastructure as demand for AI services grows.

But the expansion of AI also raises questions about who sets the rules for the technology. A report highlights the apparent contradiction surrounding OpenAI President Greg Brockman, who advocates AI safeguards even as a political group backed by $25 million from him and his wife opposes regulations that could constrain AI development. The debate underscores the tension between responsible AI development and the industry's push for innovation.

Meanwhile, cybersecurity concerns are putting digital trust under the spotlight. eMudhra is facing scrutiny after weak intermediate certificate authority keys raised concerns about website security. The issue has prompted protective measures from browser operators, while the company has said its Indian digital-signature and eSign services remain unaffected.

Adding to these concerns, a purported leak of 3,897 SBI customer records has raised fresh questions about the security of sensitive financial information and claims of data circulating on the dark web.

In today’s newsletter, we will talk about 

  • Eternal Q2 net profit rises 92% in FY27, revenue up 78% 
  • ‘You are all born artists’: Prakash Belawadi  

Here’s your trivia for today: The RBI once served as the central bank of two other countries. Which were they? (Scroll down for the answer)

News

Eternal Q2 net profit rises 92% in FY27, revenue up 78%

Eternal, the parent company of Zomato and Blinkit, reported a 92.3% year-on-year rise in net profit to Rs 125 crore in Q2 FY27, while revenue grew 78% to Rs 24,138 crore. Blinkit continued to drive growth, with net order value rising 79.3% and adjusted EBITDA turning profitable. However, Eternal's net profit fell short of analysts' estimates, even as its food delivery business recorded 21.5% growth in net order value. 

Key takeaways: 

  • Eternal’s Q2 FY27 net profit rose 92.3% YoY to Rs 125 crore, while revenue increased 78% to Rs 24,138 crore. 
  • Blinkit’s net order value grew 79.3% YoY, and adjusted EBITDA reached Rs 184 crore, compared with a loss of Rs 156 crore a year earlier. The platform added 308 stores, taking its total to 2,751.
  • Net order value at Zomato's food delivery business increased 21.5% YoY, with growth acceleration continuing for five consecutive quarters. 

TechSparks

‘You are all born artists’: Prakash Belawadi on surviving the AI age 

Actor and theatre artist Prakash Belawadi explored what artificial intelligence (AI) can and cannot replace in human creativity and work. He urged people to reconnect with their inner artist and find purpose beyond commercial success. As AI reshapes jobs and industries, he emphasised the importance of lived experience, individual expression and using technology to improve lives.

Key takeaways: 

  • Creativity is not limited to professional artists; creating for personal fulfilment has value beyond money or career prospects, said Belawadi. 
  • While AI can perform many commercially driven creative tasks, human experiences and perspectives remain important distinctions.
  • Developers should use technology responsibly to solve real-world problems, improve lives in their communities and contribute to a better India.
